hints: Think about what type of compound phenol behaves as toward sodium, compare it to the reaction of water or an alcohol with sodium and what gas is released.
walkthrough:
See phenol as an acid toward sodium**
Picture $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ with its $\text{O-H}$ group. Just like water or ethanol, that $\text{O-H}$ proton is acidic enough to be removed by reactive sodium metal. Sodium is oxidised and hydrogen is reduced, so you always get hydrogen gas and a salt.

Write the balanced salt formation**
The $\text{H}$ of the $\text{OH}$ is replaced by $\text{Na}$ to give sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$. Two phenol molecules are needed to give one $\text{H}_2$ molecule, so per mole of phenol: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$$

hints: Recall how strongly the $\text{OH}$ group activates the benzene ring and which positions it directs an electrophile to, even under dilute conditions.
walkthrough:
Remember how reactive phenol is**
The lone pair on the $\text{OH}$ oxygen is delocalised into the ring, making phenol far more reactive than benzene toward electrophiles. That means dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ alone is enough to nitrate, no concentrated acid needed, and substitution happens where the $\text{OH}$ group directs.

Place the nitro groups ortho and para**
The $\text{OH}$ group is 2,4 directing. So one product has $\text{NO}_2$ next to $\text{OH}$ at the 2 position, that is 2-nitrophenol, and the other has $\text{NO}_2$ opposite $\text{OH}$ at the 4 position, that is 4-nitrophenol. Draw both as a benzene ring bearing $\text{OH}$ plus one $\text{NO}_2$ in the ortho position and in the para position.
Final answer: Two structures: 2-nitrophenol (benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and ortho $\text{NO}_2$) and 4-nitrophenol (benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and para $\text{NO}_2$).

hints: Identify the nucleophile and the electrophile here, think about which atom in $\text{O=C=O}$ is electron deficient and how you would show that polarity.
Recall the general two stage pattern for electrophilic substitution on an activated ring, attack to break aromaticity then loss of a proton to restore it.

Look at the final product in Fig. 9.3 to work backwards, the new $\text{COO}^{-}$ group ends up ortho to $\text{O}^{-}$, so the intermediate must have both groups plus a hydrogen on that same carbon with disrupted aromaticity.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophile**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^{-}$ the ring is even more activated because of the full negative charge on oxygen. $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{O=C=O}$, looks symmetrical but each $\text{C=O}$ is polar. Oxygen is more electronegative, so label $\delta^{+}$ on carbon and $\delta^{-}$ on oxygen. That $\delta^{+}$ carbon is the electrophile that the electron rich ortho carbon will attack.

Make the first bond and draw the intermediate**
Draw a curly arrow starting inside the benzene ring and pointing to the $\delta^{+}$ carbon of $\text{CO}_2$. At the same time one $\text{C=O}$ pi bond breaks onto oxygen. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond at the ortho position. Aromaticity is temporarily lost. Draw the intermediate as a six membered ring with two double bonds only, bearing $\text{O}^{-}$ still attached, plus on the tetrahedral ortho carbon both H and the new $\text{COO}^{-}$ group.

Restore aromaticity by losing $\text{H}^{+}$**
That tetrahedral carbon still carries the hydrogen that was originally there. Draw a curly arrow from that $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to reform the pi system. The $\text{H}$ leaves as $\text{H}^{+}$. This rearomatisation gives the doubly charged product shown, with $\text{COO}^{-}$ ortho to $\text{O}^{-}$, plus $\text{H}^{+}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\delta^{+}$ C of $\text{CO}_2$ ($\delta^{-}$ on O); intermediate is non-aromatic cyclohexadienyl anion with $\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{COO}^{-}$ plus H on the attacked ortho carbon; curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform aromatic ring with loss of $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Remember this is a concerted reaction with no intermediate, three pi bonds reorganise at once in a circle to make one new pi bond and two new sigma bonds.
walkthrough:
See the circle of electron movement**
Line up buta-1,3-diene in its cisoid shape next to ethene. You need to make a six membered ring, so two new sigma bonds will join the ends of the diene to the two carbons of ethene, and the three pi bonds will shuffle into one pi bond in the product. Draw three curly arrows all pointing round in the same direction, one from each pi bond to its new position, showing simultaneous bond making and breaking to give cyclohexene.
Final answer: Three curly arrows in a cycle: from C1=C2 of diene to form C2-C3, from C3=C4 of diene to form bond to ethene, and from C=C of ethene to form bond to diene, giving cyclohexene.

hints: Apply the same Diels-Alder joining pattern as in (c)(i), but now the ethene double bond is locked inside a five membered ring, so think about what extra ring will remain fused to the new six membered ring.
walkthrough:
Join the diene across the cyclic double bond**
Treat 3-methylcyclopentene just like ethene, its $\text{C=C}$ provides the two atoms that add to the ends of buta-1,3-diene. The four diene carbons plus those two alkene carbons become a new six membered ring with one remaining $\text{C=C}$ from the diene. Because those two carbons are already part of a five membered ring, you get a fused system, a six membered ring sharing two carbons with the five membered ring, with the methyl group still on the five membered portion.
Final answer: Fused bicyclic product: new six-membered ring containing one C=C fused across the original C=C of 3-methylcyclopentene, retaining the methyl substituent on the five-membered ring.
